model: OpenAI Codex, GPT-6 family; primary dissertation editor and independent GPT-6 readers
prompt: Read the full chapters against the historical marked examples and their context. For each possible recurrence, identify the sentence a robotics, biomechanics, or neuroscience colleague cannot interpret, the earlier reader question it resembles, the evidence that would answer it, and whether the current paragraph already answers it. Apply Ben's -1 wording, -2 substantive, -3 factual/interpretive scheme to proposed inspection priorities only. Verify actual claims and identify substantive differences from the historical case. On reread, answer the reader's question from the revised text. Reserve 4/4 for explicit human confirmation. For each figure and table, compare its order and signal timing with the narrative, native data, and printed page. Test a proposed CAD change independently of a completed experiment. Read a printed chapter as a first-time reader. For each program or model, identify it and its role from the first encounter. For controller variants, identify body, circuit, and experimental condition before interpreting a result. Check captions, diagrams, and table order; verify the code name and its meaning against original model files.

passages.title: Name the physical quantity being differentiated
passages.finding: Calling these force derivatives was a technical error. A route geometry calculation differentiates length with respect to joint angle and must include the moving points.
passages.original: The CAD route additionally required consistent anatomical frames, mass and inertia assignment, joint topology, and actuator attachments. The robot frame uses $x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right. CAD assembly placement was related to that frame through a reference datum. The four-bar knees require their loop constraints to be retained in the dynamic model. Moving and conditional muscle-route points require both geometric updates and the corresponding force derivatives; changing a route's length without accounting for that dependence would give inconsistent generalized forces. Numerical derivative and virtual-work checks test those relations before interpreting motion.
passages.proposed_and_applied: I placed the CAD assembly in its anatomical frame ($x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right) using a reference datum, assigned link masses and inertias, and retained the four-bar knee constraints. Actuator tension times a route's signed moment arm gives its joint torque. By virtual work, the moment arm is the negative derivative of route length with respect to joint angle, including the motion of attachment and via points. I checked this derivative by perturbing the angle with the same points active and recorded switches of conditional points separately.
passages.reviewer_reason: The passage gives the sign, physical meaning, finite-difference check, and the fixed-active-set condition. It retains the anatomical frame and four-bar constraints.

passages.title: Carry the three-way comparison through the Discussion
passages.finding: The earlier Discussion accurately referred to two conditions in the old Results. The independent reader also found that calling the syn6 example the opposite described a parallel finding as a contrast.
passages.original: The W2L sensory intervention illustrates the value of separate outcome measures. The model moved forward under both conditions, although contact timing fell outside the accepted range after the combined removal. In syn6, the opposite problem arose during fitting. An acceptable pattern of motor recruitment concealed a PF channel that remained active throughout the cycle. Recording the signal at the receiving layer distinguished a successful output fit from a circuit that performed its intended function.
passages.proposed_and_applied: The W2L sensory intervention illustrates the value of separate outcome measures. All three conditions produced forward movement, but heel-strike phase fell outside the accepted range only after the combined removal. In syn6, an acceptable pattern of motor recruitment likewise concealed a PF channel that remained active throughout the cycle. Recording the signal at the receiving layer distinguished a successful output fit from a circuit that performed its intended function.
passages.reviewer_reason: Forward motion occurred in all three conditions. The combined deletion alone missed the phase criterion. Likewise, good motor recruitment in syn6 concealed a continuously active PF channel. The two examples now make the same interpretive point.

passages.title: Follow the physical path from actuator tension to a design decision
passages.finding: Losses between actuator force and joint torque compared unlike quantities without showing where the joint moment comes from. The tool list also obscured the researcher's decision.
passages.original: I addressed these questions at four points in the design process. The BPA measurements determine how resting length and pressure affect available force. The isometric knee experiments identify losses between actuator force and joint torque. The Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) connects a proposed feedback pathway to the conditions in which it was observed. The neuromechanical tools let a researcher test the pathway on a specified body and measure the consequence. Figure~\ref{fig:design_workflow} shows where these results enter a new design.
passages.proposed_and_applied: I addressed these questions at four points in the design process. The actuator tests show how much tension a BPA of a given resting length can produce at a specified pressure and contraction. At the knee, that tension acts through a moment arm. The isometric tests showed how deflection under load changes the torque available from a proposed route. For controller design, I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) so a researcher can find the experiment behind a proposed feedback connection. The neuromechanical tools then let the researcher change that connection in a model and measure its effect on movement. Figure~\ref{fig:design_workflow} shows where each result enters a new design.
passages.reviewer_reason: The overview traces tension through its moment arm to torque, then takes the reader from an experimental sensory pathway to a model intervention.

passages.title: Give the measured direction of the force discrepancy
passages.finding: The words measured that length dependence hid the direction of the observation and the comparison that motivated the fit. The chapter was the grammatical actor.
passages.original: The force available from a Festo BPA depends on its resting length as well as its pressure and contraction. Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} measured that length dependence and combined a maximum-force model with a three-coefficient nondimensional force surface. A designer can therefore compare candidate lengths at the operating pressure and contraction required by a joint, within the range characterized.
passages.proposed_and_applied: Festo's sizing tool predicted that a shorter BPA would produce greater maximum force. On our isometric test jig, shorter actuators of the same diameter produced less maximum force at \qty{620}{\kPa} (Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles}, Figure~\ref{fig:Fmax_fit}). We used this measured dependence on resting length to scale a three-coefficient force surface fitted to normalized pressure and contraction. A designer can use the model to compare candidate actuator lengths at the pressure and contraction required by a joint, within the range we tested.
passages.reviewer_reason: The passage compares the sizing tool and our jig at 620 kPa, gives both directions, credits the collaborative work, and tells the designer how to use the fitted surface.

passages.title: Name the reference and the experimental scope
passages.finding: Selected human-muscle torque references left a reader unable to identify either muscle or say how the corrected route was judged.
passages.original: Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} connects the measured actuator force to the knee-axis moment. Length offsets, effective compliance in the force path, and the loss of usable BPA length during wrapping accounted for discrepancies in the rigid-body torque prediction. The shared stiffness pair describes the compliance of the loaded system, including fixtures and the loading connection. With the adopted corrections, I sized flexor and extensor routes that met or exceeded the selected human-muscle torque references at the tested knee angles. This extends earlier geometric attachment-placement work \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020} to a design checked against physical measurements.
passages.proposed_and_applied: On the biomimetic knee, the original rigid-body model overpredicted the torque from the extensor route (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}). I accounted for length offsets, compliance in the loaded force path, and the loss of usable BPA length where it wraps. The fitted stiffness pair includes the compliance of the fixtures and the loading connection. I then used the corrected model to size two routes and tested them on the knee. At the sampled angles, the flexor met or exceeded the isometric torque magnitude of the Gait2392 biceps femoris short head, and the extensor met or exceeded that of the vastus medialis. These tests extend earlier work on geometric attachment placement \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020} by checking the torque each route delivers under load.
passages.reviewer_reason: The original extensor error motivates the correction. Both routes, both Gait2392 muscles, and the sampled-angle scope of the physical comparison are explicit.

passages.title: Distinguish a fixed redirect and measure the predicted output
passages.finding: The overview attributed a force–travel trade to every pulley arrangement, including a unity redirect. It proposed verifying knee torque without measuring it.
passages.original: Pulley-assisted BPA routes trade transmitted force for tendon travel and require space for the moving elements (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_routing_extensions}). A cam or artificial patella offers a different way to change the moment arm over knee flexion. Measuring the tendon tension on either side of the contact and the angle at which contact begins or ends would test whether the designed moment arm yields the expected knee torque.
passages.proposed_and_applied: In a pulley-assisted BPA route, a fixed pulley redirects tendon tension. A multi-part tackle also changes the relation between actuator travel and insertion force and needs space for the moving pulleys (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_routing_extensions}). A cam or artificial patella can change the moment arm as the knee flexes. To test that design, I would measure knee-axis torque and tendon tension on both sides of the contact across a knee-angle sweep. Recording the angles at which the tendon engages and leaves the cam would show where any discrepancy from the predicted torque occurs.
passages.reviewer_reason: The text distinguishes a fixed redirect from a multi-part tackle. The proposed cam test measures joint torque and two tensions through a knee-angle sweep and records engagement and release.

passages.title: Give the database user a specific comparison
passages.finding: The McCrea example was already concrete. Its opening said only to inspect the experiment behind a connection.
passages.original: SADb lets a researcher start with a proposed sensory connection and inspect the experiment behind it. In the Table view, selecting \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} under \emph{Pathway} returns linked papers. The record for \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} opens a curation note, its pathway links, and the article DOI. In decerebrate cats, stimulating the plantaris nerve inhibited medial gastrocnemius motoneurons at rest. During the extensor phase of midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion, the same stimulation excited these synergist motoneurons. In an acute spinal preparation treated with clonidine, inhibition decreased without the short-latency excitation. The record also links to \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition}. Reading the original experiment shows why those two links belong together and why a controller designer would test a state-dependent group~I pathway. The stimulation recruited group~I afferents and did not isolate Ib input.
passages.proposed_and_applied: In the SADb a researcher can trace a proposed connection to the stimulus and response that support it, then compare the preparations in which the response changed. passages.reviewer_reason: The opening identifies the stimulus, response, and preparation as the reason to follow the record. The original evidence for a state-dependent group I response and the limits of Ib attribution are retained.

passages.title: Retain the reproducible knee-pulse example
passages.finding: A tool list alone does not demonstrate an experimental use.
passages.original: A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse to the extensor Ia current in one run. The pulse recruited the extensor MN. The flexor was already inactive, so the rise in extensor force accounted for the initial extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The stimulated knee extended \ang{1.09} relative to the control, peaked \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset, and met the angle and speed recovery criteria \qty{6.355}{\second} after onset. Broader MN and Ia synaptic operating ranges allowed the model to settle before the pulse. The original narrow ranges produced sustained oscillation. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the MATLAB command and the fields to inspect in the saved summary.

passages.title: Retain the mechanical-power proposal
passages.finding: A generic list of future experiments would leave the output and its use unspecified.
passages.original: Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. Its timing and magnitude distinguish a knee that supplies energy during extension from one that resists motion to absorb a landing load. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.
passages.proposed_and_applied: Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.
passages.reviewer_reason: The existing passage gives signed torque and velocity, instantaneous power, an interpretation for delivery and absorption, and the required instruments. No further change was needed.

passages.title: Model sequence
passages.original:
\caption[Mechanical models and actuators]{Mechanical models, actuator formulations, and the experiments for which they were used.}
Single-joint knee and arm & Antagonist reflex circuits with simplified knee actuators or BPA20 arm actuators & Pulse the knee sensory current or raise the load in the cup. \\
Li--Deng and W2L walkers & Shared RG in the original transfer, bilateral controllers in later W2L models & Compare suspended and released motion, then test contact coordination on a supported treadmill. \\
Gait2392 human & Biological muscles driven by named graded or spiking controllers & Compare forces at matched poses and evaluate each controller in its specified physical task. \\
Gait2392 robot counterpart & Robot-specific paths with selectable muscle or BPA force laws & Test a change of force law on the routed robot. Suspended cycling used Hill-type muscles. \\
CAD robot & SNS timing and engineering allocation to 54 ideal tension actuators & Test contact handover and swing clearance under measured assistance. \\
passages.finding: Table 6.1 started with the reduced knee and arm before the walkers that motivated the work.
passages.proposed_and_applied: \caption[Mechanical models and actuators]{Mechanical models in order of introduction, with the actuator and observation used in each experiment.}
passages.reviewer_reason: Seven rows follow Li–Deng, bilateral W2L, the human reference, its rerouted robot counterpart, the CAD robot, the knee, and the arm.

passages.title: Robot routes
passages.original:
For the human-model route, I converted the Gait2392 reference from OpenSim to MuJoCo with MyoConverter. The robot counterpart required separate preparation because its artificial-muscle routes could not be combined with unchanged human-muscle parameters. Biological-muscle actuators were retained in the human reference, while robot routes and BPA forces were handled through explicit interfaces. The human model retains 92 actuator entries; six small hip-rotator entries remain disabled. The knee retains OpenSim's flexion-negative convention.
For BPA actuation, my interface evaluates the quasi-static force law from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} at the current routed length and commanded pressure and applies tensile force along the route. This allows a researcher to change the force law while retaining the mechanical geometry. The calculation assumes that commanded pressure is available at the actuator. Valve filling and loading-history effects require separate measurements.
passages.finding: The transition from a human muscle path to a robot route did not name the source, generated file, or the law used in the suspended result.
passages.proposed_and_applied: I next used \path{gait2392_robotbody.osim} to represent the routes proposed for the robot. In my earlier design I had moved actuator origins, insertions, and via points to respect the usable BPA contraction and avoid interference \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,morrow_optimization_2020}. My preparation script mirrored the intended right-side routes to the left and wrote \path{gait2392_robot.osim} for conversion. Applying human muscle parameters to the new paths caused equilibrium failures because the routed lengths had changed. With converted Hill-type actuators, the robot model cycled its legs in suspension. To test a BPA on the same geometry, I supplied a separate force law.
passages.reviewer_reason: The text follows gait2392_robotbody.osim through bilateral route preparation to gait2392_robot.osim. It identifies the Hill-type suspended example and the separate pressure-dependent BPA interface.

passages.title: CAD loading
passages.original:
CAD robot & SNS timing and engineering allocation to 54 ideal tension actuators & Test contact handover and swing clearance under measured assistance. \\
{\interlinepenalty=10000 On the separately assembled CAD robot, an SNS supplied timing while an engineering controller allocated posture, loading, and clearance targets among 54 ideal reference-tension actuators (Figure~\ref{fig:ah001_supported_control}). Over $16\leq t<28$\,s, the model produced seven qualifying right and six qualifying left swings with measured vertical assistance of \qty{77.5}{\percent} of body weight. Lateral and attitude guidance remained active. Minimum knee flexion across the complete \qty{28}{\second} trial was \ang{11.20} on the right and \ang{5.10} on the left. These results test contact handover with prescribed tensile actuation. The separate BPA interface evaluates force from length and pressure.\par}
passages.finding: The intermediate draft implied a causal test of whether loading itself cleared the swing foot.
passages.proposed_and_applied: I kept the actuator choice explicit when testing the CAD model. In the supported stepping experiment an engineering controller distributed reference tensions among 54 actuators while the SNS set their timing. This let me test whether one foot accepted load while the other unloaded and cleared the ground. The pressure-dependent BPA interface serves a different experiment, in which the available tension depends on the commanded pressure and current route length.
passages.reviewer_reason: The supported CAD experiment checks stance loading and contralateral unloading and clearance together. Its 54 ideal tensions are distinguished from a pressure-derived force.

passages.title: Retest after CAD
passages.original:
I used two routes to prepare the mechanics. For imported musculoskeletal models, I converted OpenSim geometry and muscle paths with MyoConverter and checked the result in MuJoCo. For CAD assemblies, I used joint frames, inertial properties, and attachments to assemble mechanisms for Simscape Multibody or, separately, MuJoCo. A researcher can also run a Simulink controller against existing MuJoCo mechanics through the runtime bridge. That route exchanges commands and measurements at each update and requires an executable MuJoCo model.
I placed the CAD assembly in its anatomical frame ($x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right) using a reference datum, assigned link masses and inertias, and retained the four-bar knee constraints. Actuator tension times a route's signed moment arm gives its joint torque. By virtual work, the moment arm is the negative derivative of route length with respect to joint angle, including the motion of attachment and via points. I checked this derivative by perturbing the angle with the same points active and recorded switches of conditional points separately.
passages.finding: “Repeat the same controller input” could imply clamped sensory feedback or a completed matched CAD experiment.
passages.proposed_and_applied: Figure~\ref{fig:sns_design_fit_workflow}A follows two connections in the saved left-leg W2L circuit. One PF neuron excites the extensor motor pool and the other excites the flexor pool. Moving an attachment in CAD can change its moment arm. In a model with length feedback, it can also change the stretch signal returned to the circuit. To test such a revision, I would update the attachment and its actuator and sensor mapping, then run both models with the same saved circuit, external drive, and load. Comparing their actuator forces and joint angles would show how the change affected the closed-loop response.
passages.reviewer_reason: The proposed test holds circuit, external drive, and load fixed, recomputes feedback from each body, and compares force and angle. Stretch applies in models with length feedback.

passages.title: Retest and optimization diagrams
passages.original:
I adapted the four calibration operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}. I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned entrainment under expected afferent input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how well the network reproduces the estimated activation pattern.
For repeated searches I used bounded parameters, tied left and right homologues where symmetry was intended, and used tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates. The scripts save parameters, objective components, and the termination condition. A promising candidate is rerun in a fresh process with its fitted parameters before an intervention is introduced.
passages.finding: The graphical controller and parameter search needed the workflows used in the defense.
passages.proposed_and_applied: \caption[Controller retesting and staged parameter optimization]{(A) Two left-leg pathways in the W2L Simulink circuit provide an example of what the graphical editor exposes. The CAD sequence at right shows how to repeat a controller test with revised geometry. (B) For each neural function or physical task, I specify the target, run bounded trials, and retest the selected settings.}
passages.reviewer_reason: Slide 70 shows the saved W2L connections and CAD retest. Slide 71 supplies the three optimization operations. Both citation contexts point to Figure 6.6.

passages.title: Search sequence
passages.original:
I adapted the four calibration operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}. I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned entrainment under expected afferent input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how well the network reproduces the estimated activation pattern.
For repeated searches I used bounded parameters, tied left and right homologues where symmetry was intended, and used tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates. The scripts save parameters, objective components, and the termination condition. A promising candidate is rerun in a fresh process with its fitted parameters before an intervention is introduced.
passages.finding: The earlier headings separated the design problem from the procedure that answers it.
passages.proposed_and_applied: With a circuit and mechanical model that I could run from a script, I replaced hand tuning with a sequence of parameter searches (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_design_fit_workflow}B). I chose a measurable target for one function, set bounds on the parameters that could affect it, ran the candidates, and tested the selected settings again. The target changed as I progressed from rhythm generation to muscle recruitment and then to a loaded movement.
passages.reviewer_reason: The reader can select a function, identify a target, bound a search, inspect the measurements, and replay a fitted candidate. The chapter preserves the unsuccessful calibration cases.

passages.title: Conclusion
passages.original: I developed a way to carry a controller from a circuit diagram to a mechanical test with an identifiable input and output. A future researcher can repeat the sensory pulse at the knee, disable a pathway on a supported walker, or compare the timing of a PF signal before and after closing the loop. The task, actuator law, and assistance determine which conclusions each of those experiments supports.
passages.finding: The earlier assistant draft called the reader “A colleague.” Ben had already written “A future researcher” in the supplied export.
passages.proposed_and_applied: Restoring the Gait2392 muscle-force scales gave me a human reference for recruitment tests. The BPA model predicts tension from pressure and routed length. In the same \qty{16}{\second} Gait2392 trial, sparse neural execution cut the wall time for the full process from \qty{199.624}{\second} to \qty{29.284}{\second}. A future researcher can edit a pathway or muscle route, fit the controller, and repeat the same test to measure the change in force and motion.
passages.reviewer_reason: The conclusion uses Ben’s term, identifies repaired human muscle scales and the BPA force calculation, scopes the wall-time pair, and explains the test a future researcher can repeat.

passages.title: Appendix force agreement
passages.original: Eight of twelve right-side muscles had $R^2$ between 0.87 and 0.98 and mean MuJoCo forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of OpenSim. For biceps femoris short head, a squared shape correlation of 0.868 concealed its large force-scale error. The altered rectus femoris path is one candidate explanation for its discrepancy.

passages.title: AnimatLab
passages.original: In AnimatLab, Morrow and I tuned our first walker by changing currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and running the model again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.
passages.finding: The opening used AnimatLab as a familiar program name.
passages.proposed_and_applied: Morrow and I built our first simulated walker in AnimatLab, a graphical program that couples a neural circuit to a moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. To tune the walker, we changed currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and ran it again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.
passages.reviewer_reason: The opening now identifies graphical software coupling a neural circuit to a moving body and describes the variables Morrow and Bolen adjusted.

passages.title: Li–Deng and CPG
passages.original: For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. A shared rhythm generator (RG) drove pattern-formation (PF) pathways and motor neurons (MNs) on both sides. Antagonist Hill-type muscles acted on the thighs, shanks, and feet. I added a passive toe joint. Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Its legs cycled in suspension and the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}).
passages.finding: The study names, RG, and PF identified a source without explaining which parts produced the rhythm or timed the muscles.
passages.proposed_and_applied: For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019}, a neural circuit that produces rhythmic motor commands. passages.title: MuJoCo and SNS-Toolbox

In a later walker model, W2L, the bilateral circuits received heel and toe contact signals from the simulated feet during supported treadmill stepping. I ran the controller in SNS-Toolbox, a Python library for simulating the neurons and synapses of a synthetic nervous system (SNS) \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Connecting the two programs let me change a pathway and repeat a trial under the same mechanical conditions.
passages.reviewer_reason: The physics engine calculates motion and contact. The Python library simulates the neurons and synapses coupled to it.

passages.title: Cross-program W2L test
passages.original: A contact-driven W2L test compared a 26-neuron Simulink rhythm core with the corresponding four RG signals in the 95-neuron NumPy network. passages.proposed_and_applied: To test the W2L rhythm generator across programs, I compared four RG signals in a 26-neuron Simulink circuit with their counterparts in a 95-neuron NumPy network. Warm-kernel values are medians of three blocks; the evaluator diagnostic is one paired \qty{16}{\second} stage-4 trial.}
passages.finding: A compact-backend label carried assumptions about both the balance pathway and the recurrent motor pathway.
passages.proposed_and_applied: In the second timing test, Hunt-PT+RC used a Peterka--Ting-inspired balance pathway (PT) that responds to motion of the model's center of mass. Its Renshaw cells (RC) receive motor-neuron input and feed inhibition back to the same motor pool. I compared sparse execution with a compact version that reuses working arrays and calculates ionic current only for channels with nonzero conductance.
passages.reviewer_reason: The center-of-mass balance and Renshaw recurrent-inhibition pathways are described before Table 6.4. Its 1,033-cell comparison uses a separate pair of implementations.

passages.title: Transfer experiment
passages.original: The syn6 result motivates a specific transfer experiment. Record the same PF channel first under prescribed sensory input and then during closed-loop motion. Compare the timing of transmitted output and the knee state when the two responses diverge. This would distinguish a failure of the neural timing circuit under altered input from a mechanical limit that a well-timed command cannot avoid.
passages.finding: The longer discussion pushed the second half of the conclusion onto an otherwise empty page in an intermediate proof.
passages.proposed_and_applied: I would record the same syn6 PF channel under prescribed sensory input and again during closed-loop motion. Comparing its transmitted signal and the knee state when the traces diverge would show whether sensory input alters the timing or a well-timed command reaches a mechanical limit.
passages.reviewer_reason: The two proposed experiments keep the prescribed and closed-loop cases, their observations, and the role of pressure and tendon compliance. The full conclusion now fits on printed page 162.
